'''Pascale Françoise Xavier Cossart''' ({{IPA|fr|paskal kɔsaʁ}}; née '''Gheerbrant'''; born 21 March 1948) is a French [[bacteriologist]] who is affiliated with the [[Pasteur Institute|Pasteur Institute of Paris]]. She is the foremost authority on ''[[Listeria monocytogenes]]'',<ref name="Sedwick pp. 904–905">{{cite journal | last=Sedwick | first=Caitlin | title=Pascale Cossart: The ins and outs of Listeria | journal=Journal of Cell Biology | publisher=Rockefeller University Press | volume=192 | issue=6 | date=21 March 2011 | issn=1540-8140 | doi=10.1083/jcb.1926pi | pages=904–905| pmid=21422225 | pmc=3063141 }}</ref> a deadly and common food-borne [[pathogen]] responsible for [[encephalitis]], [[meningitis]], [[bacteremia]], [[gastroenteritis]], and other diseases.

== Biography ==
Cossart was born in the north of France in 1948.  She grew up and attended school in [[Arras]].<ref name="Cossart">{{cite journal |last1=Cossart |first1=Pascale |title=Raising a Bacterium to the Rank of a Model System: The Listeria Paradigm |journal=Annual Review of Microbiology |date=15 September 2023 |volume=77 |issue=1 |pages=1–22 |doi=10.1146/annurev-micro-110422-112841 |language=en |issn=0066-4227|doi-access=free |pmid=37713460 }}</ref>
Cossart earned a B.S. and M.S. from [[Université Lille Nord de France|Lille University]] in 1968. She then earned an M.S. in chemistry from [[Georgetown University]] in 1971, and her Ph.D. in [[biochemistry]] at the Pasteur Institute and the [[University of Paris]] in 1977 ([[University Paris Diderot]]).<ref name=HHMIProfile>{{cite web |title=Pascale F. Cossart, PhD |publisher=Howard Hughes Medical Institute |url=http://www.hhmi.org/scientists/pascale-f-cossart |accessdate=19 April 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170613072124/http://www.hhmi.org/scientists/pascale-f-cossart |archive-date=13 June 2017 |url-status=dead }}</ref>  She completed her postdoctoral fellowship at the [[Pasteur Institute]].<ref name=HHMIProfile/> She is currently a Professor and Head of the Unité des Interactions Bactéries Cellules at the Pasteur Institute.<ref name=HHMIProfile/> In 1998, she received the [[Richard Lounsbery Award|Richard Lounsbery Prize]] and the [[L'Oréal-UNESCO Award for Women in Science]].<ref name=HHMIProfile/> She was awarded the [[Balzan Prize]] for Infectious Diseases: Basic and Clinical Aspects in 2013.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Balzan Prizewinners 2013 |date=9 September 2013 |publisher=International Balzan Prize Foundation |url=http://www.balzan.org/en/press-releases/news-detail/the-balzan-prizewinners-2013 |accessdate=19 April 2016 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20140717120757/http://www.balzan.org/en/press-releases/news-detail/the-balzan-prizewinners-2013 |archivedate=17 July 2014 }}</ref>

== Works ==
Cossart's research has focused on infection by [[Intracellular parasite|intracellular bacteria]], and in particular the infectious agent ''[[Listeria monocytogenes]]''.<ref name=HHMIProfile/>

''Listeria'' is a [[food-borne illness|food-borne]] bacterial [[pathogen]] responsible for numerous illnesses and a mortality rate of 30%.  The bacteria is one of the best models of [[obligate intracellular parasite|intracellular parasitism]] because it is particularly hardy, able to survive in a variety of cells, cross multiple host barriers, and spreads through [[ActA]], the protein responsible for [[actin-based motility]].<ref>[http://www.ascb.org/files/0612profile.pdf "Pascale Cossart"], ''ASCB Newsletter'', Dec. 2006, pp.32–34.</ref>  Cossart's work has shed light on the genetic and biochemical processes that make ''Listeria'' so effective and lethal, identifying the ''[[Bacillithiol|bsh]]'' gene; regulatory mechanisms such as an [[RNA]] thermosensor that control [[gene expression|expression]] of the virulence genes such as bsh; and the ways in which ''Listeria'' enters cells and crosses physiological barriers such as the [[blood–brain barrier]], the intestinal barrier, and the [[placenta|placental barrier]].  The discovery by Cossart's lab of the interaction between ''L. monocytogenes''' protein, [[internalin]], and its cell receptor, [[cadherin|E-cadherin]], was the first such study that successfully demonstrated the molecular mechanism that permits a bacterial agent to cross the placental barrier.<ref name="Cossart"/>

In 2009 Cossart published what she describes as the first "bacterial [[operon]] map"—the [[gene transcription|transcriptional program]] that regulates Listeria's behavior in different environmental conditions.<ref>''Nature'', 17 May 2009.</ref> By comparing the sequences of Listeria drawn from soil and drawn from the human gut, Cossart identified [[non-coding RNA]]s that contribute to Listeria's virulence, identified additional RNA [[repressor]]s, and determined that [[riboswitch]]es can act both downstream and upstream.<ref name="Cossart"/>

As part of her work she has also developed important biological tools, including a [[transgenic]] mouse that was the first animal model to overcome bacterial species-specificity.  The mouse carried a human version of a host cell membrane receptor that ''L. monocytogenes'' used to enter cells.<ref name="Cossart"/>
